query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An engineered surface modification that promotes the in-situ formation and regeneration of a lubricious oxide tribofilm on the CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy will continuously lower the coefficient of friction and reduce wear rates across room temperature to 800 °C under varied loads and environmental conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without any surface modification, exhibiting suboptimal tribological performance over the full temperature range.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled surface treatment (coating or modification) designed to trigger reactive oxidation such that an adaptive, self-replenishing lubricious oxide layer (tribofilm) forms during sliding.
generation.conditions: Ball-on-disk sliding tests conducted across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, under both low and high normal loads, and in representative environmental atmospheres (e.g., ambient air).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an in-situ, nanocomposite oxide tribofilm at the alloy surface that continuously reforms during sliding contact.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding conditions, the engineered surface promotes controlled oxidation with environmental oxygen. This reaction generates a deformable and strong oxide nanocomposite (tribofilm) that acts as a solid lubricant, thereby reducing metal-to-metal contact, lowering friction, and minimizing wear. The tribofilm's capability to adapt and regenerate under varying loads and temperatures is key to maintaining performance across the operating range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi material, the surface-modified sample will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and reduced wear rates at room temperature up to 800 °C, even when load and environmental conditions are varied.
generation.baseline: Tribological data from the untreated or as-processed CoCrFeNi alloy showing higher friction coefficients and elevated wear rates, particularly at temperature extremes and under high loads.
generation.boundary: Effectiveness is expected within the temperature range of room temperature to 800 °C; performance outside of this range, or in drastically different environmental conditions (e.g., ultra-high vacuum) where oxidation may be suppressed, may not follow the predicted behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of tribofilm formation and regeneration, and the long-term stability of the oxidative layer under cycling load and temperature variations, remain uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy samples: one set with the engineered surface modification and a control set of unmodified material. Conduct standardized ball-on-disk sliding tests across a temperature gradient from room temperature to 800 °C, under both low and high normal loads in ambient air.
measurements: Coefficient of friction measured in real-time during sliding
Wear volume and specific wear rate determined post-test via profilometry and microscopy
Surface characterization (e.g., SEM, XPS) to verify the formation and stability of the oxide tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the surface-modified samples do not consistently show significantly lower coefficients of friction and reduced wear rates compared to the control samples across the full temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C) and under varying load conditions, or if the adaptive tribofilm fails to form or regenerate as indicated by surface analyses, then the hypothesis is falsified.

In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. In summary, we propose a strategy to design wear-resistant alloys through in-situ formation of strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surfaces during wear, a process which we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. A representative bcc structured (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy was developed, which yields a two orders of magnitude lower wear rate than the reference TiNbZr alloy. Upon wear in ambient air, the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy forms an in-situ 400-nm-thick amorphous-crystalline nanocomposite surface layer, through reaction with the environmental O, comprising an amorphous Ti17Nb13Zr13Fe2O55 matrix containing ~10-nm-sized Ag nanocrystals. decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy systems first focused on tailoring the inherent bulk microstructure – through alloying, grain size refinement, and second-phase formation – to improve high‐temperature strength and then extended these ideas to tribological applications. Reactive wear protection strategies emerged in alloys (e.g., the TiNbZr-Ag system in PMC8448869) where controlled in-situ oxidation formed a strong, deformable oxide nanocomposite surface that reduced friction and wear at elevated temperatures. More recently, work such as PMC10241162 has demonstrated that creating adaptive heterostructured surfaces (for instance, nanohierarchical architectures) can lead to ultra-low wear rates spanning room temperature up to 800 °C. However, while these surface or interface interventions have been effective in related systems, the precise mechanisms enabling continuous low friction and wear performance across the entire temperature range in a CoCrFeNi matrix remain unresolved.
decision.unsolved: For the CoCrFeNi system the challenge is to develop a single, robust intervention that can continuously trigger the formation (and regeneration) of a lubricious tribofilm as environmental conditions, load, and temperature change. While adaptive oxide or nanocomposite layers have been engineered in other alloys, it is not clear how to reliably initiate such a reaction in the CoCrFeNi matrix without compromising its intrinsic properties across the broad sliding temperature regime.
decision.lever: engineered surface modification designed to promote in-situ formation of an adaptive, self-replenishing lubricious oxide (tribofilm) layer
decision.why: Following the trend from bulk compositional and processing modifications toward exploiting reactive surface phenomena, this intervention proposes a coating or surface treatment that triggers a controlled oxidation process. This adaptive tribofilm is expected to maintain a low coefficient of friction and wear rate from room temperature to 800 °C under varied loads and environments. Its design draws directly from prior evidence of reactive wear protection and adaptive friction interface protection, providing a clear, falsifiable experiment: if the treated CoCrFeNi samples do not exhibit sustained low friction and wear within the stated boundaries during controlled sliding tests relative to the untreated material, the hypothesis would be refuted.
